title: Valmiki and the name said backwards
hookLine: a robber can't bring himself to say Rama's name, so seven sages teach it to him backwards
carry: nama japa: the name works, even said backwards
tomorrow: what came out of Shiva's drum?

lines: A ROBBER ON THE FOREST ROAD.
cards: Before he wrote the Ramayana, Valmiki was a robber. That's how he tells it himself, in a later Sanskrit retelling called the Adhyatma Ramayana. He lived among hunters and robbed travelers on the forest road.
One day seven sages came down that road, and he raised his weapon. The sages didn't run. They asked him one question.
Your family eats what you steal. Will they share the weight of what you've done? Go and ask them.

teach.h: EVERY ONE OF THEM SAID NO.
teach.b: He went home and asked. Every one of them said no: that's yours. He came back shaken and fell at the sages' feet.
They gave him the name of Rama to repeat, but in the telling they gave it to him backwards: mara. The way the story is usually explained, he was too far gone even to say it straight.
Say mara, mara, mara, over and over, and listen.

teach.h: MARA, MARA: IT TURNS INTO RAMA.
teach.b: It turns into Rama, Rama. He sat and repeated it so long that an anthill, a valmika, rose up over his body. When the sages came back and called him out of it, he had a new name, for the anthill: Valmiki.

It's called nama japa, repeating the name of God, and many Hindus hold it as the simplest practice there is, and one of the strongest. The robber didn't have to be good first. He didn't even have to say it right.

The name did its work anyway. That's why some devotees fill whole notebooks writing Shri Rama, a practice called likhita japa, written japa, and why the name is said at the start of a journey and at the end of a life.
Now listen to the name itself. Written carefully, Rāma has a small line over the first a. That line marks length, matra, the measure of a sound in time.
A short vowel takes one measure; a long one about two.
Rāma is long, then short: Raah-muh. Chanted again and again, that long ā is where the voice rests.

how: Many Hindus practice nama japa, repeating a name of God aloud, silently, or in writing (likhita japa, filling notebooks with 'Shri Rama'); the story of Valmiki the robber, changed by repeating the name, is told to show that anyone may begin. Reciters also keep the long and short vowels of the name, as in Rāma.

s: in the Adhyatma Ramayana, Valmiki was a robber before he wrote the Ramayana
seven sages turned him, and he repeated the name until an anthill covered him.
the sages made him become good before he could start repeating the name
he began as he was; the name did its work, even said backwards.
the line over the a in Rāma is decoration
it marks a long vowel, held about twice as long: matra, length.

games.q: a friend says: 'i'd chant God's name, but i'm not a good enough person yet.' by Valmiki's story, what fits?
o: start anyway; the name changed a robber who couldn't even say it right.
wait until you've fixed yourself first.
only priests should repeat the name.
games.why: the sages gave a robber the name backwards, mara, and he rose as Valmiki. nama japa doesn't wait for you to be good first.

practice: On one out-breath, say a short a, quick and soft, then a long ā, held about twice as long. Then begin the name slowly, Rāma, long then short. Or begin the robber's way, mara, mara, and let it turn.
If you pray, let this be a small japa, a few rounds; if not, just listen to the measure of the sound.

wordCard.voice: Matra. The length of a sound in time: the line over the first a in Rāma, where the voice stays longer.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: ā, the long partner of a. In transliteration it gets a line on top.
